planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall on constantly moist soil; seed needs a cold winter to break dormancy and germinates the following spring once meltwater keeps the seedbed saturated.

directions: Arrowleaf ragwort lines the seeps, aspen-shaded streambanks, and snowmelt channels of the Rocky Mountain montane and subalpine zones, often standing knee to waist high in the dappled light under aspen or spruce-fir canopy. Clusters of yellow daisy-like flowers top leafy stems from midsummer into early fall, feeding a long run of native bees and butterflies after most other mountain wildflowers have finished. In the garden it wants a bog edge, rain garden, or shaded streamside bed where the soil never fully dries, and it spreads gradually by rhizome into a loose colony rather than staying a tidy clump. Cut stems back after frost to tidy the planting, since the foliage collapses quickly once hard freezes arrive.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto humus-rich, evenly moist soil under cover of fallen leaves; seed needs a full winter chill and germinates sparsely the following spring, so patience and a protected nursery bed pay off.

directions: Broadleaf arnica forms low, rhizomatous mats across the shaded floor of aspen groves and spruce-fir stands from the montane into the subalpine zone, where its broad heart-shaped leaves carpet the ground beneath the canopy. Single bright yellow sunflower-like blooms rise just above the foliage in early to midsummer, opening soon after snowmelt while the understory is still cool and damp. It is one of the few true shade-flowering groundcovers suited to a Rocky Mountain woodland garden, spreading steadily in rich, leafy soil but resenting hot, dry exposure or heavy clay. Divide crowded patches in early spring or fall to keep the colony vigorous and to share starts, since nursery-grown plants are uncommon outside specialty native suppliers.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall and allow winter cold and freeze-thaw cycles to soften the seed coat; germination is slow and uneven, with many seedlings not appearing until the second spring.

directions: Jessica sticktight threads through the moist meadows and light aspen shade of the Rocky Mountains and Great Basin ranges, sending up branched stems hung with small, forget-me-not-blue flowers from early to midsummer. It bridges the gap between showy spring ephemerals and the later aspen-grove bloomers, and its flowers draw bumblebees and small native bees steadily through the hottest weeks of summer. Plant it along a woodland edge or dappled border where soil stays cool and lightly moist, since full sun and drought cause it to bolt and collapse early. The small bur-like seeds cling readily to clothing and fur at maturity, so site it away from paths if that nuisance matters in a home garden.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall on well-drained soil and let winter cold stratify the seed; light aids germination, so press seed into the surface rather than burying it.

directions: Eaton's fleabane grows in the gravelly, well-drained soil at the dappled margins of aspen groves and open conifer woods across the central and southern Rockies and Great Basin, where it forms low tufts of narrow leaves topped with pale lavender-to-white rayed daisies through summer. Unlike many fleabanes that demand full sun, this species thrives on the broken light at a wood's edge and tolerates the thin, rocky soil typical of montane openings. Use it along a gravel path, rock garden border, or the sunnier fringe of a shaded bed, giving it sharp drainage so winter wet does not rot the crown. Shear spent flower heads lightly to prolong bloom and keep the clump from sprawling.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall onto evenly moist soil; seed needs winter cold to germinate well and seedlings appear with spring snowmelt the following year.

directions: Leafy aster fills the moist meadows and light aspen shade of the Rocky Mountains and ranges of the Great Basin, flowering later than almost anything else in its community with showy violet-blue rays surrounding a yellow disk from late summer into fall. Its broad, leafy bracts beneath the flower heads give the species its common name and distinguish it from finer-bracted asters in the same meadows. In cultivation it rewards a partly shaded border or woodland-edge planting with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, closing out the aspen-grove bloom season just as pollinators are stocking up for winter. Deadhead or cut back after frost, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain strong flowering.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow outdoors in fall and let a winter of cold, moist conditions break dormancy; seedlings emerge with the spring thaw and establish quickly in disturbed, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Slender cinquefoil grows through aspen-grove meadows and mountain parks across the West, holding a basal rosette of deeply palmate, silvery-backed leaves that sends up wiry stems of small, bright yellow five-petaled flowers from early to midsummer. It is at home at the dappled margins where aspen shade gives way to open meadow, filling gaps between taller wildflowers without crowding them out. Plant it in a mountain-themed border or naturalized meadow with soil that stays moist through late spring and dries moderately by late summer, matching the seasonal moisture pattern of its native aspen-parkland habitat. It self-sows modestly and tolerates light foot traffic better than most meadow forbs, making it useful along informal woodland paths.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall onto rich, moist, leafy soil in shade; the seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification and germinates erratically over the following one to two springs.

directions: Western sweetroot grows thickly across the shaded floor of aspen groves and mixed conifer forest in the Rockies, Great Basin ranges, and Pacific Northwest, where its lacy, fern-like leaves and anise-scented roots carpet the ground beneath the canopy each spring. Small white flower umbels appear in early summer, followed by slender, bristly seed pods that cling to fur and fabric the way many forest-floor umbellifers do. It fills a true shade-garden niche that few showy wildflowers can match, thriving in the cool, humus-rich soil and filtered light under deciduous or mixed canopy and spreading gradually by self-sown seed into an informal drift. Leave the dried foliage standing into fall, since the ripening seed heads are part of its character in a naturalistic woodland planting.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall on moist, humus-rich soil; a full winter of cold, moist stratification is required and germination the following spring is typically sparse and uneven.

directions: Fernleaf lovage grows in the moist, shaded soil of aspen groves, subalpine meadows, and streambanks across the central and southern Rockies, its finely divided, fern-like leaves giving rise to the common name and its aromatic, celery-and-licorice-scented roots making it a close relative of the better-known osha. Flat-topped clusters of small white flowers appear in mid to late summer above the ferny foliage, drawing a steady procession of small pollinating insects. In a shaded herb bed or woodland garden it wants deep, consistently moist soil and protection from hot afternoon sun, mimicking the cool streamside and aspen-shade conditions where it is found wild. Established plants develop a long taproot and resent transplanting once mature, so choose the planting site with care from the start.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
